title: Ethereum is a Dark Forest
relevance: First public account of a 'generalized frontrunner' copying a rescue transaction; origin of the dark-forest framing.
key_quote_or_number: "Generalized frontrunners look for any transaction that they could profitably frontrun by copying it and replacing addresses with their own. They can even execute the transaction and copy profitable internal transactions generated by its execution trace." Authors' obfuscated rescue still lost: the bot swept the funds 'in the seconds after our get transaction entered the mempool'.

title: Escaping the Dark Forest
relevance: Successful rescue of ~25,000 ETH (Lien Finance) by avoiding the public mempool via SparkPool's private transaction endpoint; shows the pre-Flashbots private-routing defense.
key_quote_or_number: "the possibility of our transactions getting frontrun was very real"; funds ~25,000 ETH (~$9.6M at the time) per our summary of the article; mined privately by SparkPool (page datePublished 2020-09-24).

title: Flash Boys 2.0: Frontrunning in Decentralized Exchanges, Miner Extractable Value, and Consensus Instability
authors: Philip Daian, Steven Goldfeder, Tyler Kell, Yunqi Li, Xueyuan Zhao, Iddo Bentov, Lorenz Breidenbach, Ari Juels
venue: arXiv 1904.05234 (10 Apr 2019); IEEE S&P 2020, pp. 910-927 (venue per DBLP listing seen in search results)
relevance: Defines priority gas auctions (PGAs) and MEV; baseline for bot-vs-bot fee competition that precedes Flashbots.
key_quote_or_number: Bots 'competitively bidding up transaction fees in order to obtain priority ordering'; 'lower bound on this economy of over USD 6M to date'.

title: Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value: How dark is the forest?
authors: Kaihua Qin, Liyi Zhou, Arthur Gervais
relevance: Section V gives the first published concrete algorithm for generalized front-running ('transaction replay'): substitute the victim sender address in calldata with the adversary's, execute locally on the latest block, front-run if profitable.
key_quote_or_number: Replay needs only 'sender benefits' or 'controllable input' patterns; 188,365 profitable replayable txs (0.02% of 883,023,232) = 57,037.32 ETH (35.37M USD) over 32 months; 0.18 +/- 0.29 s to construct and verify a replay; assumed gas price = victim + 1 wei. Overall BEV 540.54M USD, 11,289 addresses.
note: Replay in this paper is naive string replacement; they note practitioners later deployed authenticated personalised contracts (see Imitation Game).

title: Frontrunner Jones and the Raiders of the Dark Forest: An Empirical Study of Frontrunning on the Ethereum Blockchain

key_quote_or_number: 'more than 11M blocks ... almost 200K attacks with an accumulated profit of 18.41M USD'. Recounts that the second (Taichi/SparkPool) rescue succeeded by 'mining their transactions privately without broadcasting them'.

key_quote_or_number: DeFiPoser-ARB avg 191.48 ETH/week, DeFiPoser-SMT 72.44 ETH/week; finds bZx attack (0.48M USD) that existed 69 days; opportunities up to 874x block reward.

title: The Blockchain Imitation Game (APE)
authors: Kaihua Qin, Stefanos Chaliasos, Liyi Zhou, Benjamin Livshits, Dawn Song, Arthur Gervais
relevance: The 'APE' paper (note: APE is Qin et al., not Zhou et al.). Generalized imitation via dynamic analysis that synthesises adversarial contracts; counted 12 proclaimed-whitehat txs (13 known attacks) among imitable txs on Ethereum; discusses countermeasures.
key_quote_or_number: Aug 2021-Jul 2022: APE could have yielded 148.96M USD (Ethereum) and 42.70M USD (BSC); imitated 13 (ETH) and 22 (BSC) known DeFi attacks; '10 of the 12 whitehat attack transactions ... are propagated to miners privately'. Countermeasures: breaking atomicity, front-running mitigation, bytecode obfuscation, imitation as defence. Notes the naive string-replace method 'no longer applies' because traders deploy authenticated personalised contracts.

title: Your Exploit is Mine: Instantly Synthesizing Counterattack Smart Contract (STING)
authors: Zhuo Zhang, Zhiqiang Lin, Marcelo Morales, Xiangyu Zhang, Kaiyuan Zhang

key_quote_or_number: STING countered 54 of 62 real exploits; 'a general front-runner defense could only handle 12'; 'almost all attacks employ' contract-level front-running protection (CFFP), most commonly msg.sender/tx.origin equality against a constant; 7 of 62 used protection not bypassable by swapping the address. STING cannot see private (Flashbots) attack txs.

title: BACKRUNNER: Mitigating Smart Contract Attacks in the Real World
authors: Chaofan Shou, Yuanyu Ke, Yupeng Yang, Qi Su, Or Dadosh, Assaf Eli, David Benchimol, Doudou Lu, Daniel Tong, Dex Chen, Zoey Tan, Jacob Chia, Koushik Sen, Wenke Lee
venue: arXiv 2409.06213 (10 Sep 2024); no peer-reviewed venue named on the arXiv page

key_quote_or_number: 158 attack txs (54 attacks, 2023-01 to 2024-05): only 18 txs intercepted by attack-frontrunning bots, rescuing < $31.5M (8.7% of losses); merely 17/158 visible in the public mempool before block broadcast (own nodes + Blocknative); >30% of rescued funds went to builders/gas in those 17; BSC honeypot ($3K): >=6 bots, 189 bids, gas 10 -> 60,000 gwei in <600 ms, 80% of rescued funds burnt; 50 of 54 exploit contracts deployed >=1 s before the attack; 4 attack txs in 1.5 years used constructor exploits; 141/158 bypass state-of-the-art frontrunning protections; deployment: $11.2M in 28 incidents in 2 months.
